*****************************
* NUMERICAL QUADRATURE DATA *
*****************************

This is an attachment to the book "P. Solin, K. Segeth 
and I. Dolezel: Higher-Order Finite Element Methods",
Chapman & Hall/CRC Press, 2003.

Copyright March 2003 Chapman & Hall/CRC Press.

VERIFICATION AND RELIABILITY OF THE DATA:

The quadrature rules below were implemented and each of them 
tested on a reasonable number of randomly-generated polynomials
of appropriate orders. Related Mathematica notebooks are 
enclosed in a separate subdirectory. The function of the notebooks
is self-explanatory - there is a separate notebook for each
polynomial order and each domain. The integration points and
weights can be found in its first part. Definition of a polynomial
test function follows (you can see the last of several ones
that we used). Algorithm for the numerical quadrature follows, 
and finally the function is integrated analytically. 
  We encourage the reader to take a minute to test some of the 
notebooks in Mathematica by himself, not only to make sure that 
the quadrature data is correct but mainly to get a feeling for 
how the quadrature rules work.
  In the unlikely case that you discover a bug, please be so 
kind to report it to solin@caam.rice.edu and solin@iee.cas.cz. 
Your help is greatly appreciated.

QUADRATURE DOMAINS:

1D: reference interval K_a
2D: reference triangle K_t,
    reference quadrilateral K_q
3D: reference brick K_B
    reference tetrahedron K_T
    reference prism K_P
(All of them were defined in Chapter 2)

STRUCTURE OF THE QUADRATURE RULES:

All quadrature rules start with the number of quadrature 
           points.
Each line: 'd' spatial coordinates of an integration point
           and the corresponding weight (d = 1, 2 or 3 is 
           the appropriate spatial dimension)
